title: Higher-order functions and closures
idea: A higher-order function takes a function or returns one. A nested function, defined inside another, keeps its outer variables alive: a closure.

analogy.text: A function made inside another leaves with a backpack of the outer variables. It opens that backpack every time it runs, wherever it is called.
analogy.breaks: The backpack holds the variables themselves, not copies of their values.

points: The function you pass is a callback; the receiver decides when to call it.
`map` transforms each item, `filter` keeps matching items, `forEach` runs code per item.
An inner function can read the variables of the function around it.
Those variables stay alive while the inner function can still be called.

steps.caption: Line 6 calls `makeAdder(5)`. JavaScript pushes a frame that holds the parameter `n`.
The inner function is created with a link to `n`. That link is the closure, so `n` now lives on the heap.
`makeAdder` returns and its frame is popped. `add5` holds the inner function, and `n` stays alive on the heap.
Line 7 calls `add5(2)`. A new frame holds `x`. The frame of `makeAdder` is gone.
`x + n`: `x` is in this frame; `n` is found through the closure. 2 + 5 is 7.
The frame is popped and 7 is printed. Another `add5` call would still find `n` as 5.

pitfalls: Pass `fn`, not `fn()`: the parentheses call it now and pass the result.
With `var` in a loop, closures share one variable and see its last value.
You cannot `break` out of `forEach`; use `for...of` when you may stop early.

quiz.why: `var i` is one shared variable. The loop ends with `i` at 3, so every arrow function returns 3.

takeaway: Pass functions in, return them out; an inner function keeps its outer variables.
